key_insight: MC Dropout confidence scores can look trustworthy while still missing clinically important segmentation errors in brain tumour regions. Standard overlap metrics like Dice are not enough to tell whether uncertainty estimates are actually reliable for patient safety.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between segmentation accuracy metrics and real-world clinical reliability, especially for identifying failures in treatment-critical tumour sub-regions in glioma MRI segmentation.
method: Evaluate voxel-level uncertainty from Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout on multiparametric MRI brain tumour segmentation.
Test whether uncertainty can flag errors specifically in clinically critical sub-regions, not just overall segmentation quality.
Compare uncertainty behavior against standard reporting metrics to uncover calibration and reliability failure modes.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this work is a reminder that high Dice scores do not guarantee safe or dependable model behavior in medical settings. It highlights the need to validate uncertainty estimation methods against clinically meaningful error detection, not just aggregate performance numbers.
visual_elements: Side-by-side brain MRI segmentation overlay showing correct vs missed tumour sub-regions.
A reliability diagram or calibration curve comparing confidence to actual error rate.
A flowchart of MC Dropout inference producing uncertainty maps over segmentation outputs.
A small dashboard with Dice score, uncertainty heatmap, and 'missed critical region' callout.
paper_title: Confidence is Not Reliability: Rethinking MC Dropout in Brain Tumour Segmentation
paper_authors: Xin Ci Wong, Duygu Sarikaya, Kieran Zucker, Marc De Kamps, Nishant Ravikumar
